questions.q: What does container orchestration automate?
options: Scheduling containers onto machines, keeping the desired number running, routing traffic, managing rollouts and reacting to failures
questions.explain: It does this continuously without a human watching.

questions.q: What does 'declarative, reconciling control system' mean?
options: You declare desired state and Kubernetes continuously works to make actual state match it
questions.explain: This is the control (reconciliation) loop.

questions.q: Where did Kubernetes come from?
options: Designed at Google (based on Borg/Omega) and donated to the CNCF in 2015
questions.explain: It is the de facto standard for containerized workloads at scale.

questions.q: Why can't shell scripts and cron jobs scale for production?
options: They don't scale past a handful of services for restarts, rollouts, load balancing and scaling
questions.explain: Orchestration automates the messy production realities.

questions.q: Which component is the only one that talks directly to etcd?
questions.explain: Every interaction goes through the API server.

questions.q: What does etcd hold?
options: The entire cluster state as a consistent key-value store
questions.explain: If etcd is lost without backup, the cluster's state is lost.

questions.q: What does the kube-scheduler do?
options: Picks a node for newly created Pods; it only decides, and the kubelet starts the container
questions.explain: It weighs resource requests, affinity rules, taints and policy.

questions.q: What does the controller manager do?
options: Runs control loops that drive actual state toward desired state
questions.explain: Examples: the Node controller and the Deployment/ReplicaSet controller.

questions.q: How does kind differ from minikube?
options: kind runs cluster nodes as Docker containers, making it fast to start and tear down and popular for CI
questions.explain: minikube runs a node in a VM or container and ships add-ons like dashboard and ingress.

questions.q: Which command starts a minikube cluster using Docker?
questions.explain: It configures kubectl to point at the new cluster.

questions.q: How do you tear a minikube cluster down completely?
questions.explain: minikube stop only stops it without deleting.

questions.q: What do both tools need as a prerequisite?
options: A container runtime such as Docker, plus kubectl
questions.explain: Docker Desktop works as the driver for both.

questions.q: What is the general shape of a kubectl command?
questions.explain: For example kubectl describe deployment my-app.

questions.q: Which section of kubectl describe is usually the fastest way to diagnose why a Pod won't start?
questions.explain: Image pull errors, failed scheduling, crash loops and failed probes show up there with timestamps.

questions.q: How do you read logs from a previously crashed container?
questions.explain: -f streams like tail -f.

questions.q: Which is preferred: create or apply?
options: apply, declaratively from a YAML file
questions.explain: create is for quick one-offs.

questions.q: What is a Pod?
options: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network namespace, scheduled together onto one node
questions.explain: Containers in a Pod can reach each other over localhost.

questions.q: What is the sidecar pattern?
options: A small helper container such as a log shipper, proxy or config reloader running alongside the main container in the same Pod
questions.explain: It's why a Pod can hold more than one container.

questions.q: Why not create bare Pods for real workloads?
options: They have no self-healing: nothing recreates one if its node dies or it's deleted
questions.explain: Use a Deployment, which manages Pods via a ReplicaSet.

questions.q: Which four top-level fields does every manifest have?
questions.explain: spec holds the desired state specific to the kind.

questions.q: What does a ReplicaSet ensure?
options: A specified number of identical Pod replicas is running at all times
questions.explain: It replaces dead Pods and deletes extras.

questions.q: What does a Deployment add on top of a ReplicaSet?
options: Rollouts: a new ReplicaSet shifts replicas gradually from the old one, with history for rollback
questions.explain: You almost always create a Deployment, not a bare ReplicaSet.

questions.q: What must spec.selector.matchLabels match?
options: spec.template.metadata.labels; a mismatch is a validation error
questions.explain: It's how the Deployment identifies which Pods belong to it.

questions.q: What triggers a new ReplicaSet and rolling update?
options: Changing the Pod template, e.g. a new image or env var
questions.explain: Scaling replicas doesn't create a new ReplicaSet.

questions.q: Why do Services exist?
options: Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs when recreated, so a Service gives a stable IP and DNS name in front of a set of Pods
questions.explain: It load-balances across the Pods currently matching its selector.

questions.q: What is the default Service type and its reach?
options: ClusterIP, reachable only from inside the cluster
questions.explain: kubectl port-forward can tunnel to it for testing.

questions.q: Which Service type opens a fixed port in the 30000–32767 range on every node?
questions.explain: It's used for simple external access in dev/test.

questions.q: What does the Endpoints object hold?
options: The live list of Pod IPs currently matching the selector
questions.explain: kube-proxy watches it to program routing rules.

questions.q: Why externalize configuration from the image?
options: Otherwise you rebuild the image for every environment or config change
questions.explain: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive data; Secrets hold sensitive data.

questions.q: How can Pods consume ConfigMaps and Secrets?
options: As environment variables or as mounted files
questions.explain: Both objects work the same two ways.

questions.q: What does envFrom.configMapRef do?
options: Injects every key in the ConfigMap as an environment variable
questions.explain: valueFrom.configMapKeyRef pulls in a single named key.

questions.q: How are Secret values stored?
options: base64-encoded (encoding, not encryption), with special handling like exclusion from describe output
questions.explain: They can also be encrypted at rest.

questions.q: What does a namespace do?
options: Partitions one physical cluster into multiple virtual clusters
questions.explain: Names only need to be unique within a namespace.

questions.q: Which resources are cluster-scoped rather than namespaced?
questions.explain: Most others live in exactly one namespace.

questions.q: How do you reach a Service named web in the staging namespace from the default namespace?
questions.explain: The short name works only within the same namespace.

questions.q: What happens when you delete a namespace?
options: Everything in it is deleted too (cascade)
questions.explain: Check before running kubectl delete namespace.

questions.q: How is the frontend exposed to the outside in the project?
questions.explain: The backend is exposed internally through a ClusterIP Service.

questions.q: What does the API backend read for credentials?
options: A hardcoded value in the image
questions.explain: Non-sensitive settings live in the api-config ConfigMap.

questions.q: Why does the project use a httpbin image as the 'API'?
options: It's a small HTTP-echo test image, so the example runs without custom app code
questions.explain: Swap in your own image in a real project.

questions.q: Why does the note say to treat the write-up as expected behavior to verify?
options: The manifests were reasoned through, not run on a live cluster, so you should apply and verify them yourself
questions.explain: It's not a guarantee.

questions.q: What happens to data in a container's writable layer on restart?
options: It's discarded and recreated from the image
questions.explain: Volumes attach external storage so data can survive.

questions.q: How long does emptyDir data live?
options: Until the Pod is removed from the node (it survives a container restart but not Pod deletion)
questions.explain: It's good for sharing files between containers in the same Pod or for scratch space.

questions.q: Why is hostPath a security concern?
options: Files dropped there are visible to anything else on that node
questions.explain: Legitimate uses are narrow, like node-level agents.

questions.q: How do PV and PVC split responsibilities?
options: A PV is the actual storage; a PVC is a Pod's request for storage
A PV is a request; a PVC is storage
questions.explain: This lets data outlive any one Pod or node.

questions.q: Why isn't one LoadBalancer Service per app enough for HTTP routing?
options: One external IP per Service gets expensive and unwieldy with many HTTP services under one domain
questions.explain: Ingress describes host/path routing in one object.

questions.q: What does an Ingress controller do?
options: Reads Ingress objects and actually implements the routing
questions.explain: It's separate software such as NGINX Ingress, Traefik or a cloud-managed one.

questions.q: What does ingressClassName: nginx do?
options: Tells Kubernetes which installed controller should watch this Ingress
questions.explain: A cluster can run several controllers.

questions.q: How is TLS termination configured in the Ingress?
options: A tls section with hosts and a secretName pointing to a kubernetes.io/tls Secret
questions.explain: Create it with kubectl create secret tls --cert --key.

questions.q: What do requests and limits each do?
options: Requests tell the scheduler what a container needs; limits cap what it may actually use
Requests cap usage; limits tell the scheduler
questions.explain: Without them the scheduler is guessing.

questions.q: How does the scheduler decide whether a Pod fits a node?
options: By summing requests of already-scheduled Pods plus this Pod's, never looking at live usage
questions.explain: The NodeResourcesFit predicate filters nodes that would exceed allocatable capacity.

questions.q: What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit versus its memory limit?
options: CPU is throttled; memory exceeding the limit gets the container OOMKilled
questions.explain: CPU limits never kill a container.

questions.q: What does cpu: 250m mean?
questions.explain: Mi/Gi are base-1024 memory units.

questions.q: What does a failing liveness probe cause?
options: kubelet kills the container and the runtime restarts it, subject to restartPolicy
The Pod is removed from the Service only
questions.explain: It's for unrecoverable-without-restart states like deadlocks.

questions.q: What does a failing readiness probe cause?
options: The Pod's IP is removed from the Service's endpoints with no restart, resuming when it passes
questions.explain: It's the right tool for temporarily being unable to serve.

questions.q: What does a startupProbe do?
options: Disables liveness and readiness probes until it succeeds, protecting slow-starting apps from premature kills
questions.explain: The example allows up to 300s to start.

questions.q: Why isn't 'container is running' the same as 'healthy'?
options: A container can be deadlocked, stuck on a dependency or still warming up while its process is alive
questions.explain: Probes let kubelet ask the application itself.

questions.q: What do maxUnavailable and maxSurge bound?
options: How many Pods may be down and how many extra Pods may exist during a rollout
questions.explain: With 6 replicas, maxUnavailable 1 and maxSurge 1.

questions.q: How does a rolling update change Pods?
options: It creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts replica counts step by step, never editing Pods in place
questions.explain: The old ReplicaSet is kept at zero for rollback per revisionHistoryLimit.

questions.q: How do you roll back to the previous revision?
questions.explain: Add --to-revision=N for a specific one.

questions.q: Why does CHANGE-CAUSE show <none>?
options: It's populated only if you set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation
questions.explain: --record is deprecated.

questions.q: What is a Helm chart?
options: A templated, versioned package of manifests
questions.explain: It solves the problem of parameterizing and versioning raw YAML across environments.

questions.q: Where do .Values come from?
questions.explain: For example --set image.tag=1.5.0.

questions.q: What is a helm rollback in terms of revisions?
options: Another upgrade creating a new revision whose target is an old revision's manifest
A special undo with no revision
questions.explain: Rollback to revision 1 produced revision 3.

questions.q: What are the three template objects mentioned?
questions.explain: Release has install-time metadata; Chart has Chart.yaml fields.

questions.q: Why not keep three full copies of every manifest for dev, staging and prod?
options: It invites drift: a fix in one copy gets forgotten in the others
questions.explain: Use Kustomize overlays or Helm values files instead.

questions.q: How does Kustomize avoid duplication?
options: A base plus per-environment overlays that reference it and layer a small patch
questions.explain: A fix to base/deployment.yaml propagates to every environment.

questions.q: What does kubectl apply -k overlays/prod do?
options: Applies the Kustomize output of that overlay directly
questions.explain: kubectl kustomize previews the merged output.

questions.q: How does Helm achieve the same idea?
options: Layered values files, e.g. -f values.yaml -f values-prod.yaml, overriding only what differs
questions.explain: It is a common base plus a small per-environment diff.

questions.q: Why isn't a Deployment the right tool for a one-time batch task?
options: It keeps a process running indefinitely and restarts it forever
questions.explain: A Job runs a Pod to successful completion, with retries, then stops.

questions.q: What restartPolicy does a Job's Pod template need?
options: Never or OnFailure; Always makes no sense
questions.explain: backoffLimit caps retries.

questions.q: What do completions and parallelism mean in a parallel Job?
options: Total successful completions needed, and how many Pods may run at once
questions.explain: 10 completions with 3 in parallel.

questions.q: What does completionMode: Indexed give each Pod?
options: A stable index (0..N-1) for partitioning work
questions.explain: NonIndexed just needs any N successful completions.

questions.q: What is the recommended order for debugging a workload?
options: get, describe (Events), logs, exec, then debug if the container won't start
questions.explain: Random kubectl get commands waste time.

questions.q: What does CrashLoopBackOff usually mean, and where do you look?
options: A PVC is unbound; describe pvc
The image is missing; check Events
The container starts then exits repeatedly; check logs --previous
questions.explain: --previous shows the crashed container's logs, not the current restart's.

questions.q: What does ImagePullBackOff usually mean?
options: Wrong image name or tag, or missing private registry auth
questions.explain: The Events section shows the pull failure.

questions.q: Why does describe's Events section often show a problem before logs do?
options: In many cases the container never even started, so there are no logs yet
questions.explain: Scheduling failures, image pulls, probes and OOM kills surface there.

questions.q: Why does the project use a single-replica StatefulSet for the database?
options: So the PVC survives Pod rescheduling with a stable name (data-shop-db-0); Deployment semantics don't fit irreplaceable state
questions.explain: Multi-replica StatefulSets are covered in Level 3.

questions.q: How does the chart differ between dev and prod?
options: values-prod.yaml overrides replicas, storage size, host and TLS
questions.explain: For example prod has 4 replicas, 20Gi and TLS on.

questions.q: What does volumeClaimTemplates do?
options: Creates a PVC for each StatefulSet replica
questions.explain: It requests storage with ReadWriteOnce from the storageClassName.

questions.q: Which components does the project combine?
options: Volumes, Ingress, Helm and multi-environment config
questions.explain: Modules 01, 02, 06 and 07.

questions.q: When do you need a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?
options: When each replica needs a stable name, DNS entry and PVC, as in databases or brokers
questions.explain: Deployment Pods are interchangeable.

questions.q: What name do StatefulSet Pods get?
questions.explain: They also get stable DNS names through the headless Service.

questions.q: What happens when postgres-1 is deleted?
options: A Pod named postgres-1 is recreated and reattaches to the same PVC
questions.explain: Each Pod has its own PVC from volumeClaimTemplates.

questions.q: Why does a StatefulSet need a headless Service (clusterIP: None)?
options: It is required for StatefulSet DNS
questions.explain: serviceName must match it.

questions.q: What are the two separate questions every API request answers?
options: Authentication (who are you) then authorization (what can you do)
questions.explain: RBAC is the standard authorization mechanism.

questions.q: Which ServiceAccount does a Pod use if none is specified?
options: The namespace's default one, which has essentially zero permissions
questions.explain: ServiceAccounts give identity to Pods, not people.

questions.q: What does a Role plus RoleBinding grant?
questions.explain: log-reader can read Pods in prod but nothing in staging.

questions.q: When do you use ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding?
options: For cluster-wide resources like nodes or reusable permissions
questions.explain: The example grants node-reader to a monitoring ServiceAccount.

questions.q: What is the default Kubernetes networking behavior?
options: Any Pod can reach any other Pod on any port, across namespaces
questions.explain: A NetworkPolicy restricts this.

questions.q: When is a NetworkPolicy actually enforced?
options: Only if the CNI plugin implements it, such as Calico or Cilium
questions.explain: On a CNI that ignores it, the object is inert.

questions.q: What does an empty podSelector with no rules mean in the default-deny policy?
options: Select every Pod and allow nothing
questions.explain: Policies are additive, so layer allow policies on top.

questions.q: What does allow-web-to-api permit?
options: Inbound TCP 8080 to app: api Pods only from app: web Pods in the same namespace
questions.explain: Everything else stays blocked by default-deny.

questions.q: What does HPA change versus VPA?
options: HPA changes replicas; VPA changes resource requests/limits
HPA changes requests; VPA changes replicas
questions.explain: Horizontal means more copies; vertical means more CPU/memory per copy.

questions.q: What does HPA need to read CPU utilization?
options: The metrics-server add-on (or a custom metrics adapter)
questions.explain: It serves the metrics.k8s.io API from kubelet stats.

questions.q: What does averageUtilization: 70 mean?
options: Keep average CPU across replicas at 70% of each Pod's CPU request
questions.explain: Without a request, the utilization percentage has no denominator.

questions.q: What is an External metric type used for?
options: A metric with no direct Pod association, like a queue depth
questions.explain: Type Pods reads a per-Pod metric through an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter.

questions.q: Why isn't kubectl logs enough at scale?
options: It doesn't survive Pod deletion, doesn't aggregate across replicas and gives no historical trends
questions.explain: Production observability needs metrics, logs and traces.

questions.q: How does Prometheus collect metrics?
options: It pulls: discovers targets via the Kubernetes API and hits each target's /metrics endpoint
questions.explain: The app exposes Prometheus text format using a client library.

questions.q: What does kube-state-metrics add over metrics-server?
options: It turns object state (replica counts, Pod phase, PVC binding) into Prometheus metrics, while metrics-server exposes only current CPU/memory
questions.explain: For example kube_deployment_status_replicas_available.

questions.q: What do the prometheus.io/scrape annotations do?
options: Mark a Pod as a scrape target and say which port and path to use
questions.explain: The relabel config keeps only Pods annotated scrape: "true".

questions.q: What is the thundering herd problem with readiness probes?
options: If every replica's probe depends on a shared downstream, a brief blip can make all replicas unready at once, so the Service loses all backends
questions.explain: It's strictly worse than one Pod being briefly unavailable.

questions.q: What is the recommended fix?
options: Keep readiness shallow and handle downstream failures with retries/circuit breakers in app code
questions.explain: A deep /ready that pings the database couples the fleet's availability to it.

questions.q: What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?
options: Voluntary disruption such as node drains and cluster upgrades evicting too many replicas
questions.explain: Probes handle involuntary failures like crashes.

questions.q: Why jitter initialDelaySeconds?
options: So replica probes don't all fire in the same tick, which matters as probes add load at fleet scale
questions.explain: It isn't a native field; stagger via Helm or rely on rolling-update timing.

questions.q: How do multi-tenancy and multi-cluster differ?
options: Multi-tenancy is isolation within a cluster; multi-cluster is blast-radius and locality across clusters
questions.explain: They are often combined but are different decisions.

questions.q: Which building blocks make up soft multi-tenancy?
questions.explain: They suit trusted tenants like internal teams.

questions.q: Why is namespace isolation 'soft'?
options: All tenants share the same kernel, kubelet and control plane, so a container escape could cross boundaries
questions.explain: It stops accidental interference and enforces fairness.

questions.q: What is the stronger option for untrusted tenants?
options: A separate cluster or a virtual cluster per tenant
questions.explain: vcluster gives each tenant its own API server on a shared node pool.

questions.q: What is the order for write requests to the API server?
options: Authentication → authorization → admission control → persisted to etcd
questions.explain: Admission is content-aware, unlike RBAC.

questions.q: How does admission differ from RBAC?
options: RBAC asks whether an identity may do a verb; admission asks whether this specific object with these fields is acceptable
questions.explain: RBAC has no concept of object content.

questions.q: What gap do dynamic admission webhooks fill?
options: Custom logic beyond the plugins compiled into the API server
questions.explain: ResourceQuota, LimitRange and DefaultStorageClass are built-in plugins.

questions.q: What does a validating webhook respond with?
options: allowed: true or false with an optional reason, in an AdmissionReview
questions.explain: The example rejects Pods without memory limits.

questions.q: What does the Kubernetes networking model require?
options: Every Pod gets its own IP, can reach any other Pod's IP without NAT, and sees its own IP as others do
questions.explain: Kubernetes defines the model; a CNI plugin implements it.

questions.q: How do two Pods on the same node communicate?
options: Via veth pairs attached to a Linux bridge such as cni0, with no routing needed
questions.explain: One veth end is inside the Pod's namespace as eth0.

questions.q: What does an overlay (VXLAN) do for cross-node traffic?
options: Encapsulates Pod packets inside UDP packets addressed node-to-node, working on any underlying network at the cost of overhead
questions.explain: The routed alternative, e.g. Calico with BGP, avoids encapsulation.

questions.q: Which problem is kube-proxy's job?
questions.explain: The four problems also include external traffic via NAT, Ingress or LoadBalancer.

questions.q: What do topologySpreadConstraints with maxSkew 1 and DoNotSchedule accomplish?
options: The scheduler refuses to put a second replica on a node already holding one when enough nodes exist, making 'survives node loss' true
questions.explain: A StatefulSet alone doesn't guarantee spread.

questions.q: What does the PodDisruptionBudget add to the project?
options: The service can be safely drained for maintenance without evicting too many replicas at once
questions.explain: It protects availability during voluntary disruption.

questions.q: Which modules does the project combine?
options: StatefulSets, RBAC, NetworkPolicy, HPA, observability and PDBs
questions.explain: It builds a resilient 3-node key-value store.

questions.q: What does podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady do?
options: Creates Pods one at a time in order, waiting for each to be Ready
questions.explain: It's the default StatefulSet behavior.

questions.q: What does a CRD let you do?
options: Register a new resource type with its own schema and validation, without recompiling the API server
questions.explain: You get kubectl get/apply support immediately.

questions.q: What is an Operator?
options: A CRD paired with a custom controller that encodes operational knowledge as code
questions.explain: Backups, failover and upgrade steps are examples.

questions.q: What comes from the CRD's schema with no custom code?
options: kubectl get, RBAC rules and OpenAPI validation that rejects a missing required field
questions.explain: The controller adds behavior; the CRD alone is just API.

questions.q: What does scope: Namespaced mean for the CRD?
options: Its resources live inside a namespace
questions.explain: orders-db was created in prod.

questions.q: How does the GitOps pull model differ from the push model?
options: A controller inside the cluster watches Git and reconciles, so nothing outside needs write credentials to the cluster
questions.explain: CI only needs push access to Git.

questions.q: What do prune: true and selfHeal: true do together in ArgoCD?
options: Delete resources removed from Git and revert manual cluster edits, enforcing Git as the only source of change
questions.explain: Without them ArgoCD only reports OutOfSync.

questions.q: What is an ArgoCD Application?
options: A custom resource pointing at a Git path and a destination cluster/namespace
questions.explain: repoURL, targetRevision and path define the source.

questions.q: How is Flux structured differently?
options: A set of composable CRD-driven controllers like GitRepository and Kustomization instead of one Application object
questions.explain: It's Flux v2 (Flux CD).
